questions.stem: Typical elastic arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: Possess a thick tunica media

options.label: B
options.text: Possess a thick tunica media with many concentric, fenestrated, elastic laminae

options.label: C
options.text: Possess a thick tunica media with smooth muscle fibers

options.label: D
options.text: Possess series of valves throughout their length

options.label: E
options.text: Contract during diastole to help propel blood forward

notes.A: Elastic arteries such as the aorta have a thick media.
notes.B: Their media has many concentric, fenestrated elastic laminae.
notes.C: Smooth muscle cells lie between the elastic laminae.
notes.D: Arteries have no valves.
notes.E: Elastic recoil, not contraction, propels blood in diastole.

questions.why: Elastic arteries (the aorta and its large branches) have a thick media of fenestrated elastic laminae with smooth muscle; they stretch in systole and recoil in diastole, and have no valves.

questions.stem: Functions of the lymphatic system include:

options.label: A
options.text: Body immunity and filtration of lymph

options.label: B
options.text: Absorption of fats and collection of cellular debris

options.label: C
options.text: Drainage of tissue fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Production of lymphocytes

notes.A: Lymph nodes filter lymph and mount immune responses.
notes.B: Lacteals absorb dietary fat as chylomicrons, and lymph carries away cell debris.
notes.C: Lymphatics return excess tissue fluid to the blood.
notes.D: Lymphoid organs produce and house lymphocytes.

questions.why: The lymphatic system drains tissue fluid, absorbs fat from the gut, and filters lymph through lymphoid tissue that produces lymphocytes for immunity.

questions.stem: Lymph nodes:

options.label: A
options.text: Filter lymph and blood and have a single efferent lymphatic vessel that leaves via the hilum

options.label: B
options.text: Have afferent lymphatic vessels that enter the convex edge of the node and empty into the marginal sinus

options.label: C
options.text: Have medullary regions that are formed by irregular strands and cords of lymphoid tissue that alternate with lymph sinuses

notes.A: Lymph nodes filter lymph only; the spleen filters blood.
notes.B: Afferent lymphatics pierce the convex capsule and empty into the subcapsular (marginal) sinus.
notes.C: The medulla is medullary cords of lymphoid tissue alternating with medullary sinuses.

questions.why: Lymph enters a node through afferent vessels on its convex surface, percolates through the subcapsular, cortical and medullary sinuses, and leaves by efferent vessels at the hilum.

questions.stem: The thymic medulla contains:

options.label: A
options.text: Hassall’s corpuscles and lymphoid nodules with germinal centres

options.label: B
options.text: Central arteries and marginal zones

options.label: C
options.text: Large venous sinusoids and Billroth’s cords

options.label: D
options.text: A whirl-like arrangement of epithelial reticular cells

options.label: E
options.text: Diffuse lymphoid tissue

notes.A: Hassall's corpuscles are medullary, but the thymus has no lymphoid nodules or germinal centres.
notes.B: Central arteries and marginal zones belong to the spleen.
notes.C: Venous sinusoids and Billroth's cords belong to the splenic red pulp.
notes.D: Whorls of epithelial reticular cells form Hassall's corpuscles.
notes.E: The medulla has diffuse, paler-staining lymphoid tissue.

questions.why: The thymic medulla is pale diffuse lymphoid tissue with Hassall's corpuscles (whorled epithelial reticular cells); it has no germinal centres, central arteries or splenic cords.

questions.stem: The thymus:

options.label: A
options.text: Lacks both afferent lymphatic vessels and lymphoid nodules

options.label: B
options.text: Has a cortex and a medulla based largely on different concentrations of lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Has a capsule from which trabeculae extend into the interior of the organ to form partial lobules

options.label: D
options.text: Produces T- lymphocytes and involutes rapidly after puberty

options.label: E
options.text: Has a perivascular connective tissue sheath in the cortex that is ensheathed by the epithelial reticular cells

notes.A: It has no afferent lymphatics and no lymphoid nodules.
notes.B: The dark cortex is packed with lymphocytes; the medulla has fewer.
notes.C: Trabeculae from the capsule divide it into incomplete lobules.
notes.D: It produces T lymphocytes and involutes after puberty.
notes.E: Epithelial reticular cells ensheath the cortical vessels, forming the blood–thymus barrier.

questions.why: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ: incomplete lobules with a lymphocyte-rich cortex (protected by the blood–thymus barrier) and a paler medulla, no afferent lymphatics or nodules, and involution after puberty.

questions.stem: The spleen:

options.label: A
options.text: White pulp contains nodular regions and non-nodular regions that are comparable to the cortex of a lymph node

options.label: B
options.text: Sinuses are defined, endothelium-lined vascular channels that branch and anastomose irregularly

options.label: C
options.text: The red pulp is formed by two vascular compartments, sinuses and Billroth’s cords

options.label: D
options.text: The red pulp resembles the lymphatic sinuses and medullary cords in the medulla of the lymph node

options.label: E
options.text: Red pulp Cords are made up of a three-dimensional meshwork of reticular cells and reticular fibres with macrophages

notes.A: White pulp has nodules and periarterial lymphoid sheaths, comparable to a node's cortex.
notes.B: Splenic sinuses are endothelium-lined channels that branch and anastomose.
notes.C: Red pulp has two compartments: venous sinuses and splenic (Billroth's) cords.
notes.D: Red pulp sinuses and cords resemble a node's medullary sinuses and cords.
notes.E: Splenic cords are a reticular meshwork with macrophages that remove old red cells.

questions.why: The spleen's white pulp (lymphoid nodules and periarterial sheaths) handles immunity, while the red pulp (venous sinuses and macrophage-rich Billroth's cords) filters blood.

questions.stem: All of the following about the spleen are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Is the site of the largest accumulation of lymphoid tissue in the human body

options.label: B
options.text: Is the site of destruction of red blood cells

options.label: C
options.text: Is for the production of lymphocytes and immune responses

options.label: D
options.text: Contains plasma cells, macrophages and reticular fibers

options.label: E
options.text: Contains venous sinusoids which act as the main filters of foreign particles

questions.why: Filtering is done mainly in the marginal zone and splenic cords; sinusoids are channels.

notes.A: True.
notes.B: True.
notes.C: True.
notes.D: True.

questions.stem: Functions performed by EVERY lymphoid organ:

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration of lymph

options.label: B
options.text: Production of lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Destruction of blood cells

options.label: D
options.text: Filtration of blood

options.label: E
options.text: Production of reticular fibers

notes.A: Only lymph nodes.
notes.C: Spleen only.
notes.D: Spleen only.
notes.E: The thymus has none.

questions.why: All lymphoid organs produce (or house proliferating) lymphocytes; filtration roles differ.

questions.stem: The jejunum differs from the duodenum mainly by the ABSENCE of:

options.label: A
options.text: Relatively large submucosal collections of lymphoid tissue in its submucosa known as Peyer’s patches

options.label: B
options.text: Simple, test-tube shaped invaginations of the mucosa known as crypts of Lieberkuhn

options.label: C
options.text: Prominent plicae circulares

options.label: D
options.text: Brunner’s glands

options.label: E
options.text: Chief cells

questions.why: Brunner's (submucosal) glands mark the duodenum.

notes.A: Ileum.
notes.B: Both have crypts.
notes.C: Both have plicae.
notes.E: Stomach.

questions.stem: Swell bodies of the nasal conchae perform all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Sensory perception

options.label: B
options.text: Adjustment of the temperature of inspired air

options.label: C
options.text: Regulation of blood flow to the overlying epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing contact between inspired air and the nasal mucosa

options.label: E
options.text: Increasing pressure in the nasal cavity

questions.why: Swell bodies warm air and adjust flow; they have no sensory role.

notes.B: A function.
notes.C: A function.
notes.D: A function.
notes.E: A function.

questions.stem: The nasal cavity has:

options.label: A
options.text: 3 bony shelf-like projections known as conchae/turbinates

options.label: B
options.text: An inferior concha covered by a specialized olfactory epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Superior and middle conchae covered by respiratory epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: Turbinates which increase the surface area and cause turbulence in airflow to allow more efficient conditioning of inspired air

options.label: E
options.text: Narrow, ribbon-like passages created by the conchae resulting in increased contact between the Streams of air and the mucous layer

notes.A: There are three conchae: superior, middle and inferior.
notes.B: The superior concha carries the olfactory epithelium, not the inferior.
notes.C: Only the middle and inferior conchae are respiratory; the superior is olfactory.
notes.D: Conchae increase surface area and create turbulence to warm and humidify air.
notes.E: The narrow meatuses bring air into close contact with the mucus.

questions.why: The three conchae increase mucosal surface area and turbulence; the superior concha carries olfactory epithelium, while the middle and inferior are covered by respiratory epithelium.

questions.stem: Paranasal sinuses:

options.label: A
options.text: Are air-filled spaces in the bones of the walls of the nasal cavity

options.label: B
options.text: Are located in the ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal, maxillary, palatine and lacrimal bones

options.label: C
options.text: Are lined with a thinner respiratory epithelium that contains goblet cells

options.label: D
options.text: Communicate with the nasal cavities via narrow openings onto the respiratory mucosa

notes.A: They are air spaces in the bones around the nasal cavity.
notes.B: The sinuses are frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary; none are in the palatine or lacrimal bones.
notes.C: Their respiratory epithelium is thinner, with fewer goblet cells.
notes.D: Each opens into the nasal cavity by a narrow ostium.

questions.why: The paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary) are air spaces lined by thin respiratory epithelium that drain into the nasal cavity through narrow openings.

questions.stem: The pharynx:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a musculofibrous half-cylinder that links the oral and nasal cavities to the larynx and oesophagus

options.label: B
options.text: Serves as a passageway for air and food and provides a resonating chamber for speech

options.label: C
options.text: Diffuse lymphatic tissue and lymphatic nodules are found in its wall

options.label: D
options.text: Is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblets and stratified squamous non- keratinized epithelium

options.label: E
options.text: Is connected to the middle ear by the auditory (Eustachian) tubes

notes.A: It is a fibromuscular half-tube, open in front to the nose, mouth and larynx.
notes.B: It carries air and food and acts as a resonating chamber for speech.
notes.C: Its wall has lymphoid tissue, including the tonsils.
notes.D: The nasopharynx has respiratory epithelium; the oro- and laryngopharynx have non-keratinised stratified squamous.
notes.E: The auditory tubes open into the nasopharynx.

questions.why: The pharynx carries both air and food, so its lining changes from respiratory epithelium in the nasopharynx to stratified squamous where food passes, with lymphoid tissue (tonsils) guarding the entrance.

questions.stem: The larynx:

options.label: A
options.text: Is an air passage, an organ of phonation and a sphincteric mechanism that closes the lower respiratory tract

options.label: B
options.text: Is part of the respiratory portion of the respiratory system

options.label: C
options.text: Has three unpaired hyaline cartilages; cricoid, thyroid and epiglottis

options.label: D
options.text: Has three pairs of elastic cartilages; arytenoids, corniculates and cuneiform

options.label: E
options.text: Has a fibroelastic membrane and numerous intrinsic skeletal muscles

notes.A: It conducts air, makes sound and closes as a sphincter to protect the airway.
notes.B: It belongs to the conducting portion; gas exchange starts at the respiratory bronchioles.
notes.C: The epiglottis is elastic cartilage; the thyroid and cricoid are hyaline.
notes.D: The arytenoids are mainly hyaline; the corniculates, cuneiforms and arytenoid tips are elastic.
notes.E: It has fibroelastic membranes and intrinsic skeletal muscles.

questions.why: The larynx is a conducting airway with hyaline cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, most of the arytenoids) and elastic ones (epiglottis, corniculate, cuneiform), moved by intrinsic skeletal muscles.

questions.stem: The epiglottis:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a leaf-shaped cartilage attached by its stem to the posterior aspect of the thyroid cartilage at the thyroid angle

options.label: B
options.text: Has below it, a pair of mucosal folds that lack muscle and are covered by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblets

options.label: C
options.text: Contains mixed mucous and serous glands and hyaline cartilage

notes.A: Its stalk attaches to the back of the thyroid angle.
notes.B: The vestibular (false) folds below it are mostly glands and loose connective tissue with little or no muscle, unlike the vocal folds, and are covered by respiratory epithelium.
notes.C: Its glands are mixed, but its cartilage is elastic, not hyaline.

questions.why: The epiglottis is a leaf of elastic cartilage attached to the thyroid angle; below it lie the vestibular (false) folds, which are mainly glands and connective tissue rather than muscle.

questions.stem: Bronchi:

options.label: A
options.text: The wall of the bronchi is structurally similar to the mucosa of the trachea except for the organization of cartilage and smooth muscle,

options.label: B
options.text: Are air passages for air conduction, filtration and warming

options.label: C
options.text: Have a band of muscle reinforced with elastic fibres at the junction of the submucosa and lamina propria

notes.A: They resemble the trachea except that cartilage forms plates and smooth muscle forms a complete layer.
notes.B: They conduct, filter and warm air.
notes.C: A smooth muscle layer with elastic fibres lies between the lamina propria and submucosa.

questions.why: Bronchi keep the trachea's respiratory mucosa but have irregular cartilage plates and a continuous smooth-muscle layer between the lamina propria and submucosa.

questions.stem: Bronchioles:

options.label: A
options.text: Are intralobular airways with diameters of 1 mm or less without cartilages and glands

options.label: B
options.text: Have pseudostratified columnar ciliated with goblet cells or simple columnar ciliated with goblet cells and simple cuboidal ciliated epithelium with Clara cells

options.label: C
options.text: Have a relatively thick layer of smooth muscle

options.label: D
options.text: Have Clara cells that secrete a surface-active agent, a lipoprotein to prevent luminal adhesion

options.label: E
options.text: Has a muscularis that is under the control of the vagus nerve and the sympathetic nervous system

notes.A: Bronchioles are 1 mm or less and have no cartilage or glands.
notes.B: The epithelium changes from ciliated columnar with goblet cells to cuboidal with Clara (club) cells.
notes.C: Their smooth muscle layer is relatively thick for their size.
notes.D: Clara (club) cells secrete a surfactant-like lipoprotein that stops the walls sticking.
notes.E: The vagus constricts and sympathetic nerves dilate them.

questions.why: Bronchioles lack cartilage and glands, so their relatively thick, autonomically controlled smooth muscle sets airway calibre; club (Clara) cells replace goblet cells distally.

questions.stem: Respiratory bronchioles:

options.label: A
options.text: Have walls that are interrupted by numerous alveoli for gas exchange

options.label: B
options.text: Have simple cuboidal ciliated epithelial cells with Clara cells and simple squamous epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Have smooth muscle and elastic connective tissue

options.label: D
options.text: Are continuous with terminal bronchioles and alveolar ducts

options.label: E
options.text: Have Type I alveolar cells

notes.A: Alveoli open from their walls, so some gas exchange happens here.
notes.B: Cuboidal ciliated cells with Clara cells line them, becoming squamous at the alveolar openings.
notes.C: Smooth muscle and elastic fibres lie between the alveolar openings.
notes.D: They lie between the terminal bronchioles and the alveolar ducts.
notes.E: Type I cells line the alveoli in their walls.

questions.why: Respiratory bronchioles are transitional: a cuboidal bronchiolar wall interrupted by alveoli, linking terminal bronchioles to alveolar ducts.

questions.stem: Alveoli:

options.label: A
options.text: Have a lining of Type I and II Alveolar Cells and Occasional Brush Cells

options.label: B
options.text: Form the mass of the parenchyma of the lung, giving the appearance of fine lace or a sponge

options.label: C
options.text: Are the terminal air spaces of the respiratory system and are the actual sites of gas exchange Between the air and the blood

options.label: D
options.text: Have very thin squamous cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface

options.label: E
options.text: Have cuboidal secretory cells covering about 5% of the surface, mainly at septal junctions

notes.A: They are lined by type I and II cells with occasional brush cells.
notes.B: They form most of the lung parenchyma, giving its spongy look.
notes.C: They are the terminal air spaces where gas exchange takes place.
notes.D: Type I cells cover about 95% of the surface.
notes.E: Type II cells cover about 5%, mainly at septal junctions.

questions.why: Alveoli are the gas-exchange spaces: thin type I cells cover about 95% of the surface and cuboidal type II cells, which make surfactant, the rest.

questions.stem: Pulmonary surfactant:

options.label: A
options.text: Forms a monomolecular layer over the alveolar epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Reduces the surface tension at the air-epithelium interface

options.label: C
options.text: The alveoli would collapse on exhalation without adequate secretions of surfactant

options.label: D
options.text: Inadequate secretions of surfactant causes respiratory distress syndrome

options.label: E
options.text: Is secreted by the type II pneumocyte cuboidal secretory cells

notes.A: It forms a monomolecular film over the alveolar lining.
notes.B: It lowers surface tension at the air–liquid interface.
notes.C: Without it alveoli would collapse at the end of expiration.
notes.D: Deficiency, as in premature babies, causes respiratory distress syndrome.
notes.E: Type II pneumocytes secrete it from their lamellar bodies.

questions.why: Surfactant from type II pneumocytes lowers alveolar surface tension so the alveoli stay open in expiration; too little causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: The alveolar septum:

options.label: A
options.text: Consists of the Alveolar epithelial cells, Basal lamina of the alveolar epithelium, Basal lamina of the capillary endothelium, Endothelial cells of the rich capillary network

options.label: B
options.text: Consists of connective tissue elements, including fibroblasts, macrophages, collagen fibers, and elastic fibers

options.label: C
options.text: Has a thin portion consisting of a monomolecular layer of surfactant, a type I epithelial cell, a capillary endothelial cell and the fused basal lamina

options.label: D
options.text: Has a thick portion consisting of connective tissue cells and fibers between the two basal laminae

options.label: E
options.text: Gas exchange occurs across the thin portion of the barrier whereas the thick portion is a site for accumulation of tissue fluid

notes.A: Its layers include alveolar epithelium, both basal laminae and capillary endothelium.
notes.B: Its connective tissue has fibroblasts, macrophages, collagen and elastic fibres.
notes.C: The thin portion is surfactant, type I cell, fused basal lamina and endothelium.
notes.D: In the thick portion connective tissue separates the two basal laminae.
notes.E: Gas crosses the thin portion; fluid collects in the thick portion.

questions.why: The alveolar septum has a thin portion (fused basal laminae) where gas exchange occurs and a thick portion with connective tissue where tissue fluid can collect.

questions.stem: Alveolar macrophages:

options.label: A
options.text: Remove inhaled particulate matter from the air spaces and red blood cells from the septum

options.label: B
options.text: Function both in the connective tissue of the septum and in the air space of the alveolus

options.label: C
options.text: May remain in the septal connective tissue and may stay for much of an individual’s life

options.label: D
options.text: That are filled with carbon particles are present in lungs of a smoker at autopsy

options.label: E
options.text: Phagocytose infectious organisms such as tubercle bacilli

notes.A: They clear inhaled particles from the air spaces and red cells from the septum.
notes.B: They work both in the septal connective tissue and in the alveolar lumen.
notes.C: Some stay in the septum for much of life.
notes.D: Carbon-filled 'dust cells' are seen in smokers' lungs.
notes.E: They phagocytose organisms such as tubercle bacilli.

questions.why: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) patrol the septa and air spaces, engulfing inhaled particles, microbes and red cells that leak into the septum.

questions.stem: The olfactory segment of the nasal cavity has:

options.label: A
options.text: A slight yellowish-brown colour due to the presence of pigment in the olfactory epithelium and olfactory glands

options.label: B
options.text: A pseudostratified columnar epithelium with Olfactory cells, sustentacular cells and goblet cells

options.label: C
options.text: Tubuloalveolar glands that produce a watery serous secretion for washing and trapping of odorant substances and renewal of the olfactory sensation

options.label: D
options.text: A lamina propria with olfactory nerves in combination with the olfactory glands

options.label: E
options.text: Bipolar neurons that are replaced during postnatal life

notes.A: Pigment in the epithelium and glands gives a yellowish-brown colour.
notes.B: It has basal cells, not goblet cells.
notes.C: Bowman's glands produce the serous secretion that dissolves and washes away odorants.
notes.D: The lamina propria contains olfactory nerve bundles and Bowman's glands.
notes.E: Olfactory neurons are replaced from basal cells throughout life.

questions.why: Olfactory epithelium is tall pseudostratified epithelium with receptor neurons, sustentacular and basal cells but no goblet cells; serous Bowman's glands wash its surface.

questions.stem: The tongue:

options.label: A
options.text: The mucosa of the ventral surface of the tongue is modified to form papillae

options.label: B
options.text: Is a mass of skeletal muscle that runs in different planes

options.label: C
options.text: Has whitish areas which are due to the presence of numerous highly keratinised filiform papillae and reddish rounded areas of fungiform papillae among the filiform papillae

options.label: D
options.text: Has glands that are interspersed among the skeletal muscle fibres

options.label: E
options.text: Has taste receptors in all the papillae

notes.A: Papillae are on the dorsum; the ventral surface has thin, smooth mucosa.
notes.B: It is skeletal muscle running in three planes.
notes.C: Keratinised filiform papillae look white; fungiform papillae look red.
notes.D: Serous and mucous glands lie among the muscle fibres.
notes.E: Filiform papillae have no taste buds.

questions.why: The tongue is interlacing skeletal muscle with glands; papillae cover only its dorsum, and the numerous filiform papillae have no taste buds.

questions.stem: The stomach has:

options.label: A
options.text: Peptic cells which secrete pepsin and intrinsic factor

options.label: B
options.text: A mucus-secreting epithelium which helps to protect the gastric mucosa from autodigestion and its own highly acidic secretion

options.label: C
options.text: Gastric pits that serve as short ducts for conveying gastric secretions from the mucosal glands to the lumen of the stomach

options.label: D
options.text: Parietal cells secrete HCL, gastrin and Pepsin

options.label: E
options.text: Rugae that are composed of the mucosa and the underlying submucosa

notes.A: Chief cells make pepsinogen; parietal cells make intrinsic factor.
notes.B: Surface mucous cells secrete an alkaline mucus that protects the mucosa.
notes.C: Gastric pits are short ducts into which the glands open.
notes.D: Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor; G cells make gastrin.
notes.E: Rugae are folds of mucosa and submucosa that flatten when the stomach fills.

questions.why: Chief cells make pepsinogen, parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor, and G cells make gastrin; surface mucus protects the mucosa.

questions.stem: A loop of small intestine is identified as jejunum rather than ileum because the:

options.label: A
options.text: Jejunum has a greater diameter and a thicker wall due to the plicae circulares

options.label: B
options.text: Jejunal arterial arcades are simple or double with long vasa recti while the ileal arcades are Multiple with short vasa recti

options.label: C
options.text: Ileum has shorter club-shaped villi

options.label: D
options.text: Ileum contains more goblet cells and ileal mesentery contains more fat making it opaque

options.label: E
options.text: Ileum has more lymphoid nodules

notes.A: The jejunum is wider and thicker-walled, with tall, close plicae.
notes.B: Jejunal arcades are few with long vasa recti; ileal arcades are many with short vasa recti.
notes.C: Ileal villi are shorter and club-shaped.
notes.D: The ileum has more goblet cells, and its fatty mesentery is opaque.
notes.E: The ileum has large lymphoid aggregates (Peyer's patches).

questions.why: Jejunum is wider and thicker, with tall plicae, few arcades and long vasa recti; ileum has short villi, more goblet cells, Peyer's patches, a fatty mesentery and many arcades.

questions.stem: Following a barium meal in a normal person, the outline of the barium shadow in the first part of the duodenum was smooth. In the remaining parts of the duodenum. The barium was broken up, giving a floccular appearance. These differences in appearance are due to the:

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of plicae circulares in the first part of the duodenum and numerous plicae circulares in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of lymphoid nodules in the first part of the duodenum and numerous lymphoid nodules in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of plicae circulares in the first part of the duodenum and absence of plicae circulares in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: D
options.text: Absence of villi in the first part of the duodenum and numerous villi in the remaining parts of the duodenum

options.label: E
options.text: Absence of muscle in the first part of the duodenum and a prominent muscle layer in the remaining parts of the duodenum

questions.why: The duodenal cap has no plicae circulares, so barium outlines it smoothly.

notes.B: Not the cause.
notes.C: Reversed.
notes.D: Villi are everywhere.
notes.E: Muscle is everywhere.

questions.stem: The liver:

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatocytes are bathed by arterial and venous blood entering the liver via the hepatic artery and the portal vein respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Sinusoidal blood flows away from the central vein

options.label: C
options.text: Blood from the central vein ultimately drains into the inferior vena cava via the hepatic veins

options.label: D
options.text: Sinusoidal blood spaces are lined by discontinuous endothelial and Kupffer cells

options.label: E
options.text: Between two directly adjacent hepatocytes is a bile canaliculus

notes.A: Hepatocytes receive mixed blood from the hepatic artery and portal vein.
notes.B: It flows toward the central vein.
notes.C: Central veins drain to sublobular and then hepatic veins into the IVC.
notes.D: Sinusoids have discontinuous endothelium with Kupffer cells.
notes.E: Bile canaliculi run between adjacent hepatocytes.

questions.why: Mixed arterial and portal blood flows through sinusoids (discontinuous endothelium, Kupffer cells) toward the central vein and on to the IVC, while bile flows the opposite way in canaliculi.

questions.stem: Both a muscularis mucosae and a myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus are present in:

options.label: A
options.text: Uterus, uterine tube and vas deferens

options.label: B
options.text: Duodenum, ureter, tongue and epididymis

options.label: C
options.text: Ureter, oesophagus, ejacutory ducts, trachea

options.label: D
options.text: Jejunum, stomach, duodenum and oesophagus

options.label: E
options.text: Penis, gallbladder, urinary bladder and urethra

questions.why: Only the gut has both a muscularis mucosae and a myenteric plexus.

notes.A: Not gut.
notes.B: Ureter, tongue, epididymis are not gut.
notes.C: Not gut.
notes.E: Not gut.

questions.stem: All of the following about the lips are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The lips serve for suckling

options.label: B
options.text: The lips are associated with speech

options.label: C
options.text: The lips are responsible for keeping food in the mouth

options.label: D
options.text: The lips do not have muscular tissue

options.label: E
options.text: The lips are similar in structure to the cheeks

questions.why: The lips contain orbicularis oris.

notes.A: True.
notes.B: True.
notes.C: True.
notes.E: True.

questions.stem: The glomeruli are best described as being tufts of

options.label: A

options.text: Posterior to the inferior border of the symphysis pubis and the pubic arch and serves as a site of spermatozoa storage and maturation

options.label: C
options.text: The largest accessory sex gland that secretes fibrinoysin, Acid phosphatase and citric acid

options.label: D
options.text: Has acidophilic smooth muscle cells between the secretory alveoli and acidophilic concretions within the alveoli

notes.A: It has a fibromuscular stroma.
notes.B: It does not store sperm.
notes.C: It is the largest accessory gland and secretes fibrinolysin, acid phosphatase and citric acid.
notes.D: Smooth muscle lies between the alveoli, and acidophilic concretions (corpora amylacea) lie within them.

questions.why: The prostate is the largest accessory gland: tubuloalveolar glands in a fibromuscular stroma that secrete citric acid, fibrinolysin and acid phosphatase, often with prostatic concretions in the alveoli.

questions.stem: After vasectomy:

options.label: A
options.text: Penile erection is possible

options.label: B
options.text: Normal sexual relations are impaired

options.label: C
options.text: Spermatozoa may be found in the ejaculate for 60 days or more

options.label: D
options.text: Production of spermatozoa continue to old age

options.label: E
options.text: Fertility is impaired

notes.A: Erection depends on nerves and blood flow, which are unaffected.
notes.B: They are not.
notes.C: Weeks to months.
notes.D: The testes keep making sperm, which are reabsorbed.
notes.E: Once stored sperm clear, sperm cannot reach the ejaculate, so fertility is impaired.

questions.why: Vasectomy blocks sperm transport but not hormones or erection; sperm production continues, and stored sperm can appear in the ejaculate for weeks, so fertility ends only once it is clear.

questions.stem: The ejaculatory duct:

options.label: A
options.text: It has no muscle in its wall; the fibromuscular tissue of the prostate substitutes for its muscularis

options.label: B
options.text: Its muscular coat consists of two layer

options.label: C
options.text: It is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: It conducts sperm

options.label: E
options.text: It contains sertoli cells

notes.A: The prostatic fibromuscular tissue takes the place of a muscularis.
notes.B: No muscle coat of its own.
notes.C: It is lined by pseudostratified (or simple) columnar epithelium.
notes.D: It carries sperm from the ductus deferens to the urethra.
notes.E: Testis only.

questions.why: The ejaculatory duct runs through the prostate, carrying sperm and seminal fluid; it has no muscle coat of its own, the prostate's fibromuscular stroma serving instead.

questions.stem: The glans penis:

options.label: A
options.text: Projects backwards and laterally to cover the distal ends of the corpora cavernosa

options.label: B
options.text: Contains the fossa navicularis of the urethra that is lined with stratified columnar epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Consists only of convolutions of large veins, and it does not reach the same state of rigidity as the shaft of the erect penis

options.label: D
options.text: Consists of the urethra, three cavernous bodies and a prepuce that resembles a mucous membrane on its inner aspect

notes.A: It caps the distal ends of the corpora cavernosa.
notes.B: Non-keratinized stratified squamous.
notes.C: Its erectile tissue is convoluted veins, so it never becomes as rigid as the shaft.
notes.D: The glans contains only the corpus spongiosum, not three cavernous bodies.

questions.why: The glans is the expanded end of the corpus spongiosum, made of large convoluted veins, so it stays softer than the shaft; the fossa navicularis is lined by stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.stem: About testicular function:

options.label: A
options.text: The cooler venous blood returning from the testis and scrotum cools the arterial blood before it enters the testis

options.label: B
options.text: Dividing populations of germ cells are very sensitive to radiation

options.label: C
options.text: Prolonged residence of the testis within the abdomen results in progressive degeneration of germ cells

options.label: D
options.text: Frequent immersions in hot baths or wearing close-fitting, tight trousers may result in fewer sperm in the ejaculate

notes.A: The pampiniform plexus cools arterial blood by countercurrent heat exchange.
notes.B: Rapidly dividing germ cells are very radiosensitive.
notes.C: Body temperature in an undescended testis leads to germ-cell degeneration.
notes.D: Raised scrotal temperature can lower sperm counts.

questions.why: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature a few degrees below core, kept by the scrotum and the pampiniform plexus, and its dividing germ cells are easily damaged by heat and radiation.

questions.stem: The interstitial tissue of the testis contains:

options.label: A
options.text: A rich blood supply

options.label: B
options.text: An extensive network of lymphatic vessels

options.label: C
options.text: Fenestrated capillaries

options.label: D
options.text: Leydig cells and Call Exner bodies

options.label: E
options.text: Leydig cells and Sertoli cells

notes.A: It has a rich blood supply for hormone transport.
notes.B: It has an extensive lymphatic network.
notes.C: Fenestrated capillaries carry testosterone away from the Leydig cells.
notes.D: Call-Exner bodies are in ovarian follicles.
notes.E: Sertoli cells are inside the tubules.

questions.why: The testicular interstitium has Leydig cells among blood vessels, fenestrated capillaries and many lymphatics; Sertoli cells are inside the tubules and Call-Exner bodies are ovarian.

questions.stem: The vulva:

options.label: A
options.text: Consists of the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, vestibule of the vagina, vestibular glands and the clitoris

options.label: B
options.text: The labia minora are two elongated hairless folds that enclose the pudendal/urogenital cleft

options.label: C
options.text: The labia majora are two small hairless folds of skin located between the labia majora at either side of the opening of the vagina

options.label: D
options.text: The clitoris consists of erectile tissue that is richly innervated with sensory endings and is capable of enlargement as a result of engorgement with blood

options.label: E
options.text: The clitoris is traversed by the urethra

notes.A: These are the parts of the vulva.
notes.B: The labia majora enclose the cleft.
notes.C: That describes the labia minora.
notes.D: The clitoris is richly innervated erectile tissue that engorges with blood.
notes.E: It is not.

questions.why: The vulva is the mons, labia majora (hairy, enclosing the cleft), labia minora (hairless), vestibule, vestibular glands and clitoris; the urethra opens in the vestibule, not through the clitoris.

questions.stem: The cervical mucosa (endocervix):

options.label: A
options.text: Lacks spiral arteries and contains large branched tubular glands

options.label: B
options.text: Undergoes very little change in thickness during the menstrual cycle and is not sloughed off during menstruation

options.label: C
options.text: Secretes a fluid that is voluminous and thin in consistency at ovulation and can be penetrated by spermatozoa more readily

options.label: D
options.text: Secretes a thick mucoid product that acts as a barrier to sperm transport in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle

options.label: E
options.text: Blockage of the openings of the cervical glands results in the retention of their secretions and formation of dilated cysts known as Nabothian cysts

notes.A: It lacks spiral arteries and has large branched glands.
notes.B: It changes little during the cycle and is not shed at menstruation.
notes.C: At ovulation oestrogen makes the mucus thin and abundant, easy for sperm to cross.
notes.D: In the luteal phase progesterone makes the mucus thick, a barrier to sperm.
notes.E: Blocked gland openings trap secretions, forming Nabothian cysts.

questions.why: The endocervix has no spiral arteries and is not shed; its branched glands make mucus that is thin at ovulation and thick in the luteal phase, and blocked glands form Nabothian cysts.

questions.stem: Uterine and ovarian changes in pregnancy:

options.label: A
options.text: The smooth muscle cells of the uterus increase greatly in length during pregnancy from 50µm to 500µm

options.label: B
options.text: There is a striking growth of the blood vessels

options.label: C
options.text: The corpus luteum persists to produce progesterone

options.label: D
options.text: The corpus luteum regresses and both progesterone and oestrogen production ceases

notes.A: Myometrial cells lengthen about tenfold.
notes.B: Uterine blood vessels grow strikingly.
notes.C: The corpus luteum persists to make progesterone in early pregnancy.
notes.D: It persists into the second trimester.

questions.why: In pregnancy the uterus grows mainly by enlargement of its smooth muscle cells and blood vessels, while the corpus luteum persists to make progesterone until the placenta takes over.

questions.stem: Lactation and fertility:

options.label: A
options.text: Lactational amenorrhoea is due to high levels of serum Prolactin

options.label: B
options.text: High serum Prolactin suppresses secretion of Luteinizing hormone

options.label: C
options.text: Resumption of ovulation occurs with a decrease in suckling frequency

options.label: D
options.text: Lactational amenorrhoea is a means of birth control

notes.A: High prolactin causes lactational amenorrhoea.
notes.B: Prolactin suppresses GnRH and therefore LH.
notes.C: Less frequent suckling lowers prolactin, allowing ovulation to resume.
notes.D: Exclusive breastfeeding is used as a natural (lactational amenorrhoea) method of birth control.

questions.why: Frequent suckling keeps prolactin high, which suppresses GnRH and LH and so ovulation; ovulation returns as suckling becomes less frequent.

questions.stem: The coiled (spiral) arteries of the endometrium:

options.label: A
options.text: Are present in the uterine cervix

options.label: B
options.text: Constrict and close off blood supply at the end of the secretory phase

options.label: C
options.text: Are found in the stratum functionalis

options.label: D
options.text: Develop again during each menstrual cycle

options.label: E
options.text: Are well developed during the mid-secretory phase

notes.A: Absent there.
notes.B: Their constriction at the end of the secretory phase makes the functionalis ischaemic.
notes.C: They supply the stratum functionalis.
notes.D: They regrow from the basalis each cycle.
notes.E: They are best developed in the mid-secretory phase.

questions.why: Spiral arteries grow in the functionalis each cycle, are best developed in the secretory phase, and constrict at its end, causing the ischaemia that leads to menstruation.

questions.stem: The cervical wall:

options.label: A
options.text: Contains a limited number of smooth muscle cells (15%) and a large amount of dense connective tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Has a complex pattern of connective tissue and smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.text: Regulates access to the uterine cavity and dilates for the emergence of the newborn

options.label: D
options.text: Consists largely of collagenous fibers, some elastic fibers along the outermost surface and relatively little smooth muscle

notes.A: Only about 15% is smooth muscle; most is dense connective tissue.
notes.B: Its connective tissue and smooth muscle are arranged in a complex pattern.
notes.C: It guards the uterine cavity and dilates for delivery.
notes.D: It is mainly collagen, with some elastic fibres and relatively little muscle.

questions.why: The cervical wall is mainly dense collagenous connective tissue with little smooth muscle (about 15%), which lets it hold the pregnancy and then soften and dilate at birth.

questions.stem: All of the following about granulosa lutein cells are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: They are the predominant cell type in the corpus luteum

options.label: B
options.text: They are derived from the theca interna

options.label: C
options.text: They contain abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: D
options.text: They are large and pale-staining

options.label: E
options.text: They secrete progesterone

questions.why: Granulosa lutein cells come from granulosa cells; theca lutein cells from the theca interna.

notes.A: True.
notes.C: True.
notes.D: True.
notes.E: True.

questions.stem: Decidual cells:

options.label: A
options.text: Differentiate from endometrial epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Secrete prolactin

options.label: C
options.text: Control the invasion of the trophoblast and acts as an immunological barrier that protects the embryo from maternal immune rejection

notes.A: They come from stromal cells.
notes.B: Decidual cells secrete prolactin.
notes.C: They limit trophoblast invasion and form an immunological barrier.

questions.why: Decidual cells are enlarged endometrial stromal cells that secrete prolactin, limit trophoblast invasion and help protect the embryo from maternal immune rejection.

questions.stem: Corpora lutea:

options.label: A
options.text: Develop after ovulation from the theca folliculi only

options.label: B
options.text: Possess both granulosa lutein cells and theca lutein cells

options.label: C
options.text: Develop under the influence of Luteininizing hormone and are yellow in appearance

options.label: D
options.text: Have lipid-rich cells and secrete both oestrogen and progesterone

notes.A: From granulosa and theca.
notes.B: It contains both granulosa lutein and theca lutein cells.
notes.C: LH drives luteinisation, and lipid gives the yellow colour.
notes.D: Its lipid-rich cells secrete progesterone and oestrogen.

questions.why: After ovulation, under LH, granulosa and theca cells become lipid-rich granulosa lutein and theca lutein cells, forming a yellow corpus luteum that secretes progesterone and oestrogen.

questions.stem: Ovarian follicular atresia:

options.label: A
options.text: May occur at any stage of follicular development

options.label: B
options.text: Is characterized by disorganization of the granulosa cells

options.label: C
options.text: Is characterized by thickening of the basement membrane between the granulosa cells and theca Interna, known as the glassy membrane

options.label: D
options.text: Is characterized by disintegration of the oocyte and persistence of the collapsed zona pellucida

options.label: E
options.text: May involve invasion of the follicle by connective tissue

notes.A: Follicles can become atretic at any stage.
notes.B: The granulosa cells become disorganised and die.
notes.C: The basement membrane thickens into a hyaline glassy membrane.
notes.D: The oocyte disintegrates, but its collapsed zona pellucida persists.
notes.E: Connective tissue may invade the degenerating follicle.

questions.why: Atresia can affect follicles at any stage: granulosa cells disorganise, the oocyte breaks down leaving the zona pellucida, a thick glassy membrane forms and connective tissue invades.

questions.stem: Variations in the wall of the uterine tube:

options.label: A
options.text: Mucosal folds reach their greatest height and complexity in the ampulla and are reduced in both Size and complexity closer to the uterus

options.label: B
options.text: Ciliated cells are usually more numerous at the infundibular end of uterine tube whereas secretory cells tend to predominate at the uterine end

options.label: C
options.text: The number of ciliated cells increase from the infundibulum to the interstitial segment whereas the number of secretory cells decrease from the infundibulum to the interstitial segment

options.label: D
options.text: Ciliated cells are more numerous during the follicular phase of the cycle, whereas secretory cells predominate during the luteal phase

options.label: E
options.text: Ciliation is progesterone-dependent

notes.A: Folds are tallest and most complex in the ampulla.
notes.B: Ciliated cells dominate at the infundibular end, secretory cells at the uterine end.
notes.C: They decrease toward the uterus.
notes.D: Ciliated cells increase in the follicular phase; secretory cells dominate in the luteal phase.
notes.E: Ciliogenesis is oestrogen-dependent.

questions.why: Uterine tube folds are tallest in the ampulla; ciliated cells dominate toward the infundibulum and in the oestrogen-dominated follicular phase, and secretory cells toward the uterus and in the luteal phase.

questions.stem: The uterus:

options.label: A
options.text: Has a functionalis which is shed at menses

options.label: B
options.text: Has a basalis that lacks glands and is adjacent to the myometrium and is retained at menstruation

options.label: C
options.text: Has a fundus that is the usual site of implantation

notes.A: The functionalis is the layer shed at menstruation.
notes.B: It contains the bases of the glands.
notes.C: The fundus (upper body) is the usual implantation site.

questions.why: The endometrial functionalis is shed at menses and regrows from the basalis, which keeps the bases of the glands; implantation usually occurs high in the body or fundus.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland:

options.label: A
options.text: Has follicles that are roughly spheroid cyst-like compartments with walls formed by a simple squamous or cuboidal epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Has follicles that are filled with a gel-like mass that contains thyroglobulin, the inactive storage form of the thyroid hormones

options.label: C
options.text: Has parafollicular cells within the follicular epithelium or scattered in the interfollicular connective tissue

options.label: D
options.text: Parafollicular cells secrete a hormone that reduces the level of calcium in the blood

options.label: E
options.text: Thyroid hormones are essential for fetal development and regulate metabolism

notes.A: Follicles are spheres walled by simple squamous to cuboidal epithelium.
notes.B: Colloid contains thyroglobulin, the storage form of the hormones.
notes.C: Parafollicular cells lie in the follicle wall or between follicles.
notes.D: They secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium.
notes.E: Thyroid hormones are needed for fetal development and regulate metabolism.

questions.why: Thyroid follicles of cuboidal or squamous epithelium store hormone as thyroglobulin colloid, and parafollicular (C) cells secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium.

questions.stem: The parathyroid glands:

options.label: A
options.text: Are usually found embedded in the thyroid gland and function in the regulation of blood ion levels of calcium and phosphate

options.label: B
options.text: Have more numerous principal/chief cells with pale-staining, slightly acidophilic cytoplasm, centrally located nuclei and large accumulations of glycogen and lipid droplets

options.label: C
options.text: Have oxyphil cells that are larger than chief cells

notes.A: They lie on the back of the thyroid, usually in its capsule.
notes.B: Chief cells are the numerous, pale, PTH-secreting cells.
notes.C: Oxyphil cells are larger than chief cells, with acidophilic, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm.

questions.why: The parathyroids lie on the back of the thyroid and regulate calcium and phosphate; chief cells (PTH) are numerous and pale, while oxyphil cells are larger and acidophilic.

questions.stem: The islets of Langerhans:

options.label: A
options.text: Contain Alpha and Beta cells

options.label: B
options.text: The alpha cells secrete insulin and the Beta cells secrete glucagon

options.label: C
options.text: Contain ducts for transport of its secretory products and rosette-shaped secretory acini

options.label: D
options.text: Are richly vascularised for transport of its secretory products

options.label: E
options.text: Secrete somatostatin

notes.A: Alpha and beta cells are the main islet cells.
notes.B: Beta cells make insulin; alpha make glucagon.
notes.C: Endocrine: no ducts.
notes.D: A rich capillary network carries their hormones away.
notes.E: Delta cells secrete somatostatin.

questions.why: Islets are ductless endocrine clusters with a rich capillary network: beta cells make insulin, alpha cells glucagon and delta cells somatostatin.

questions.stem: The adrenal gland:

options.label: A
options.text: Is organized into cortical protein-secreting and medullary, catecholamine-secreting portions

options.label: B
options.text: The cortex is the steroid-secreting portion and constitutes nearly 90% of the weight of the gland

options.label: C
options.text: The medulla is divided into Zona glomerulosa, Zona fasciculata, and Zona reticualris,

options.label: D
options.text: The cells of the zona glomerulosa are arranged in closely packed ovoid clusters whereas the cells of zona fasciculata are arranged in long straight cords separated by the sinusoidal capillaries

notes.A: The cortex secretes steroids.
notes.B: The steroid-secreting cortex is about 90% of the gland's weight.
notes.C: Those are cortical zones.
notes.D: Glomerulosa cells form ovoid clusters; fasciculata cells form long straight cords between sinusoids.

questions.why: The adrenal cortex (about 90% of the gland) secretes steroids from three zones; the medulla secretes catecholamines.

questions.stem: Junctional complexes are located on the:

options.label: A
options.text: Apical membrane only

options.label: B
options.text: Basal and lateral membranes only

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral membrane only

options.label: D
options.text: Apical and basal membranes

notes.A: Not on the free surface.
notes.B: Not basal.
notes.C: They lie on the lateral membranes, near the apex.
notes.D: Not basal.

questions.why: Junctional complexes (tight junction, zonula adherens, desmosome) sit on the lateral membranes near the apex, sealing and binding neighbouring cells.

questions.stem: An epithelium has both microvilli and cilia. It:

options.label: A
options.text: Was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses

options.label: B
options.text: Is from a surface where both absorption and motility are required

options.label: C
options.text: Is from a chamber that changes its volume continually

notes.A: That needs stratified squamous.
notes.C: Transitional epithelium.

questions.why: Cilia move things; microvilli absorb. Together they suggest absorption plus motility (e.g. efferent ductules, respiratory epithelium).

questions.stem: The lateral border between two epithelial cells carries:

options.label: A
options.text: Hemidesmosomes and desmosomes

options.label: B
options.text: Tight junctions, adhering junctions and hemidesmosomes

options.label: C
options.text: Cilia, desmosomes and zona occludens

options.label: D
options.text: Zonula occludens and zonula adherens only

options.label: E
options.text: Zonula adherens and macula adherens only

notes.A: Hemidesmosomes are basal.
notes.B: Hemidesmosomes are basal.
notes.C: Cilia are apical.
notes.D: Desmosomes and gap junctions are also present.
notes.E: Tight and gap junctions are also present.

questions.why: Lateral borders carry tight junctions, adhering junctions, desmosomes and gap junctions.

questions.stem: Epithelial cells specialized for ion transport are found in the:

options.label: A
options.text: Skin

options.label: B
options.text: Ducts of salivary glands

options.label: C
options.text: Ducts of pancreas

options.label: D
options.text: Kidney tubules

options.label: E
options.text: Choroid plexus

notes.A: Skin epithelium is protective, not ion-transporting.
notes.B: Striated ducts modify saliva by ion transport.
notes.C: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate.
notes.D: Kidney tubule cells transport ions across basal infoldings.
notes.E: The choroid plexus transports ions to make CSF.

questions.why: Ion-transporting epithelia have basal infoldings packed with mitochondria, as in striated ducts of salivary glands, pancreatic ducts, kidney tubules and the choroid plexus.

questions.stem: About epithelial tissues:

options.label: A
options.text: Junctional complexes are found at numerous sites between epithelial cells and their underlying connective tissue

options.label: B
options.text: Stereocilia are extremely long form of microvilli

options.label: C
options.text: The principal function of microvilli is to increase the surface area of cells

options.label: D
options.text: Desmosomes are sites of strong intercellular adhesion and provide points of attachment for elements of the cytoskeleton

options.label: E
options.text: Cilia constitute the characteristic brush border of the small intestine

notes.A: They join cells to each other, not to CT.
notes.B: Stereocilia are very long, non-motile microvilli.
notes.C: Microvilli mainly increase the absorptive surface.
notes.D: Desmosomes give strong adhesion and anchor intermediate filaments.
notes.E: Microvilli form the brush border.

questions.why: Microvilli increase surface area (forming the brush border), stereocilia are very long microvilli, and junctional complexes and desmosomes join epithelial cells to each other.

questions.stem: An epithelium with a striated border:

options.label: A
options.text: It has tightly packed cilia and lines the respiratory tract

options.label: B
options.text: It has tightly packed microvilli and lines the uterus

options.label: C
options.text: It has tightly packed stereocilia and lines proximal segment of the nephron

options.label: D
options.text: It has tightly packed microtubules and lines floating chorionic villi

options.label: E
options.text: It has tightly packed microvilli and covers intestinal absorptive cells

notes.A: Respiratory epithelium has cilia, which are motile and are not a striated border.
notes.B: The uterine lining has no striated border.
notes.C: The PCT has a brush border of microvilli.
notes.D: Chorionic villi are covered by trophoblast, not a microtubule border.
notes.E: Densely packed microvilli on intestinal absorptive cells form the striated border.

questions.why: A striated border is a dense layer of microvilli on intestinal absorptive cells; the similar border in the proximal tubule is called a brush border.

questions.stem: A junctional complex includes:

options.label: A
options.text: A tight junction, a desmosome and a zonula adherens

options.label: B
options.text: A zonula adherens, a desmosome and a zonula occludens

options.label: C
options.text: A gap junction, a hemidesmosome and a tight junction

options.label: D
options.text: A tight junction, a basal lamina and a terminal web

options.label: E
options.text: A basal lamina, a hemidesmosome and a gap junction

notes.B: Same components.
notes.C: No.
notes.D: No.
notes.E: No.

questions.why: A junctional complex: zonula occludens (tight), zonula adherens and macula adherens (desmosome).

questions.stem: Goblet cells are found in the lining of:

options.label: A
options.text: Stomach and gallbladder

options.label: B
options.text: Ileum, colon, trachea and respiratory bronchioles

options.label: C
options.text: Large intestine, primary bronchi and gallbladder

options.label: D
options.text: Trachea, stomach, uterus, appendix

options.label: E
options.text: Jejunum, appendix and primary bronchi

notes.A: Neither has goblet cells.
notes.B: Respiratory bronchioles have none.
notes.C: Gallbladder has none.
notes.D: Stomach and uterus have none.
notes.E: Jejunum, appendix and primary bronchi all have goblet cells.

questions.why: Goblet cells occur in intestinal and respiratory epithelium (down to the larger bronchioles), but not in the stomach, gallbladder, uterus or respiratory bronchioles.

questions.stem: An Anatomy Professor examined three different specimens from unknown locations. He concluded that specimen A was taken from a chamber that changes its volume continually, specimen B was from a surface where both absorption and secretion are required and specimen C was from an internal surface where friction may occur. Specimens A, B, C were:

options.label: A
options.text: Transitional epithelium, simple columnar epithelium with goblets and a brushborder, stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Simple columnar epithelium, simple columnar epithelium with goblets and a brushborder and stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium respectively

options.label: C
options.text: Transitional epithelium, stratified cuboidal and stratified squamous non-keratinized Epithelium respectively

options.label: D
options.text: Transitional epithelium, pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with a brushborder, stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium respectively

options.label: E
options.text: Urinary bladder, small intestine and oesophagus respectively

notes.B: A is not simple columnar.
notes.C: B is not stratified cuboidal.
notes.D: B is not pseudostratified.

questions.why: A changes volume: transitional (bladder). B absorbs and secretes: simple columnar with goblet cells and brush border (small intestine). C friction: non-keratinized stratified squamous (oesophagus).

questions.stem: A male Anatomy Professor also examined three different specimens from unknown locations. He concluded that specimen D was taken from a surface that was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses, specimen E was from a surface where either filtration or diffusion occurs and specimen F was from an internal chamber where absorption and motility are required. Specimens D, E, F were obtained from:

options.label: A
options.text: Filiform papillae of tongue, parietal layer of renal corpuscle and epididymis respectively

options.label: B
options.text: Surfaces with stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, simple squamous epithelium and pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with a brushborder respectively

options.label: C
options.text: Surfaces with stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with a brushborder and simple squamous epithelium respectively

notes.A: The epididymis has stereocilia, not motile cilia.
notes.C: Order reversed.

questions.why: D: keratinized stratified squamous. E: simple squamous. F: an epithelium with cilia and microvilli.

questions.stem: Transitional epithelium stops urine leaking between its cells through its:

options.label: A
options.text: Gap junctions

options.label: B
options.text: Tight junctions

options.label: C
options.text: Desmosomes

options.label: D
options.text: Terminal web

options.label: E
options.text: Hemidesmosomes
